title: What are the differences between REST, gRPC, and Kafka?
shortTitle: Differences between REST, gRPC, and Kafka

s1_definition.profdef: REST, gRPC, and Kafka are three different communication technologies with different models. REST is synchronous request-response over HTTP/1.1 using text formats like JSON, resource-oriented, human-readable, and universally supported. gRPC is synchronous request-response over HTTP/2 using binary protocol buffers with a strict contract defined in a `.proto` file, offering much higher performance, smaller payloads, strong typing, and bidirectional streaming, but less browser-friendliness. Kafka is not request-response at all; it is an asynchronous, durable, distributed event log where producers publish to topics and consumer groups read at their own pace, giving decoupling, buffering, replay, and very high throughput at the cost of eventual consistency. REST and gRPC answer "call me and wait"; Kafka answers "announce it and move on".
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, REST is like sending a clearly written letter in plain language to a specific counter and waiting for the reply: anyone can read it, but it is a bit bulky. gRPC is like a fast, pre-agreed coded form between two bank branches that both understand exactly: tiny, quick, and strict, but an outsider cannot read it. Kafka is like the bank's internal announcement board: a department pins a note that something happened and walks away, and any department reads it whenever it is ready. REST and gRPC are both "ask and wait at a counter"; Kafka is "post an announcement and let people react later".
s1_definition.oneliner: REST is text-based synchronous HTTP for universal, human-readable request-response; gRPC is binary HTTP/2 synchronous for fast, strongly-typed internal calls with streaming; Kafka is an asynchronous durable event log for decoupled, high-throughput, replayable fan-out.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** REST, gRPC, and Kafka are three different communication technologies with different models. REST is synchronous request-response over HTTP/1.1 using text formats like JSON, resource-oriented, human-readable, and universally supported. gRPC is synchronous request-response over HTTP/2 using binary protocol buffers with a strict contract defined in a `.proto` file, offering much higher performance, smaller payloads, strong typing, and bidirectional streaming, but less browser-friendliness. Kafka is not request-response at all; it is an asynchronous, durable, distributed event log where producers publish to topics and consumer groups read at their own pace, giving decoupling, buffering, replay, and very high throughput at the cost of eventual consistency. REST and gRPC answer "call me and wait"; Kafka answers "announce it and move on".

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, REST is like sending a clearly written letter in plain language to a specific counter and waiting for the reply: anyone can read it, but it is a bit bulky. gRPC is like a fast, pre-agreed coded form between two bank branches that both understand exactly: tiny, quick, and strict, but an outsider cannot read it. Kafka is like the bank's internal announcement board: a department pins a note that something happened and walks away, and any department reads it whenever it is ready. REST and gRPC are both "ask and wait at a counter"; Kafka is "post an announcement and let people react later".

**One line to remember:** REST is text-based synchronous HTTP for universal, human-readable request-response; gRPC is binary HTTP/2 synchronous for fast, strongly-typed internal calls with streaming; Kafka is an asynchronous durable event log for decoupled, high-throughput, replayable fan-out.

sections.s2_technical:
REST uses HTTP/1.1 and usually JSON. It is resource-oriented, so you model nouns and use verbs like GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE, for example `GET /api/v1/accounts/SAV2001`. Its strengths are universal support, human readability, easy caching, and simple tooling, which makes it the default for public APIs and browser clients. Its weaknesses are larger payloads because JSON is text, no built-in streaming in the classic model, and the overhead of HTTP/1.1. You use it synchronously and the caller blocks for the response.

gRPC also does synchronous request-response but over HTTP/2 with protocol buffers, a compact binary format. You define the service and messages in a `.proto` file and generate strongly-typed client and server stubs, so a call is a typed method, for example `accountStub.debit(DebitRequest.newBuilder().setAccountId("SAV2001").setAmount(50000).build())`. Its strengths are much smaller and faster messages, a strict contract that catches mismatches at compile time, built-in support for unary and bidirectional streaming, and multiplexing many calls over one HTTP/2 connection. Its weaknesses are poor native browser support, binary payloads that are harder to debug by eye, and the need to share and regenerate `.proto` contracts. gRPC shines for high-throughput internal service-to-service calls where latency and payload size matter.

Kafka is a fundamentally different model: an asynchronous, durable, partitioned log. Producers publish to a topic with `kafkaTemplate.send("payment-events", key, event)` and return immediately. Messages are persisted and ordered within a partition, and consumer groups read at their own pace, so many independent consumers can process the same stream. Its strengths are decoupling, because the producer does not know its consumers, buffering under load, replay because the log retains history, very high throughput, and resilience because a down consumer does not fail the producer. Its weaknesses are eventual consistency, no synchronous reply, at-least-once delivery that forces idempotent consumers, and harder end-to-end tracing.

The key differences line up on a few axes. On interaction model, REST and gRPC are synchronous request-response while Kafka is asynchronous publish-subscribe. On transport and encoding, REST is HTTP/1.1 and text, gRPC is HTTP/2 and binary, and Kafka is its own TCP protocol with a durable log. On coupling, REST and gRPC couple the caller to the callee's availability, while Kafka decouples them in time. On typical use, REST is for public and simple internal APIs, gRPC is for fast internal calls and streaming, and Kafka is for events, fan-out, and high-throughput pipelines. The senior-level nuance is that these are complementary, not competing: a real bank uses REST at the public edge, gRPC for hot internal paths, and Kafka for the event backbone, choosing per interaction rather than standardizing on one.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, one transfer touches all three technologies. Problem 1 — the mobile app, a browser-style client, must call the bank over something universal and readable, so the public edge must be REST. Problem 2 — internally, the Payment Service calls the Account Service millions of times a day for debits, and JSON over HTTP/1.1 is too slow and bulky, so this hot internal path should be gRPC. Problem 3 — after the transfer, many services must react and more will be added later, and the customer must not wait, so this fan-out should be Kafka. The mini-project shows the same transfer using the right technology at each hop.

The mini-project models a `RestEdge` for the public call, a `GrpcAccountStub` for the fast internal debit, and a `KafkaBackbone` for the event fan-out, coordinated by a `TransferOrchestrator`. A runnable demo runs a transfer that enters over REST, debits over gRPC, and broadcasts over Kafka, logging the characteristics of each.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of 50,000 rupees from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001).

Step 1: The mobile app sends the transfer as JSON to the REST edge over HTTP/1.1. REST is used because the client is external and needs a universal, human-readable, cacheable protocol. The edge accepts it synchronously.

Step 2: The orchestrator makes the internal debit call to the Account Service using gRPC over HTTP/2 with a binary protobuf message. This hop uses gRPC because it is a hot internal path where small, fast, strongly-typed messages matter, and the caller needs the confirmed result.

Step 3: The gRPC debit returns success synchronously. Because the contract is defined in a `.proto` file and generated into typed stubs, a field mismatch would have been caught at compile time rather than at runtime.

Step 4: The orchestrator publishes a `PAYMENT_COMPLETED` event to Kafka and returns immediately. Kafka is used because this is a fact being announced to many consumers that may grow over time, and the customer must not wait for any of them.

Step 5: The event sits durably in the Kafka log at a new offset. Notification, audit, and fraud consumers read it at their own pace, and because the log is replayable, a brand-new consumer added next month can read the history. The same transfer thus used REST for reach, gRPC for speed, and Kafka for decoupled fan-out.

```text
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:10 INFO === One transfer, three technologies, each where it fits ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:10 INFO REST (HTTP/1.1, JSON) received from mobile app: {"from":"SAV2001","amount":50000}
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:10 INFO gRPC (HTTP/2, binary protobuf) debit 50000 from SAV2001 — small + fast + typed
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:10 INFO Kafka (async log) → 'payment-events': PAYMENT_COMPLETED from=SAV2001 amount=50000 — producer does NOT wait, consumers read later
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:10 INFO Final result: COMPLETED
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
REST, gRPC, and Kafka are three different communication technologies, and I describe them along a few clear axes. REST is synchronous request-response over HTTP/1.1 using text formats like JSON. It is resource-oriented, human-readable, easy to cache and document, and supported everywhere, which makes it the default at the public edge for browsers, mobile apps, and third parties. Its downsides are bulkier text payloads and the overhead of HTTP/1.1, and like any synchronous call it couples the caller to the callee's availability.

gRPC is also synchronous request-response, but over HTTP/2 using binary protocol buffers with a strict contract defined in a .proto file that generates strongly-typed stubs. That gives much smaller and faster messages, compile-time safety against contract mismatches, multiplexing over one connection, and built-in streaming. The tradeoffs are poor native browser support and binary payloads that are harder to eyeball, so I use gRPC for hot internal service-to-service paths where latency and payload size really matter, not at the public edge.

Kafka is a completely different model: an asynchronous, durable, partitioned event log. Producers publish to a topic and move on, and many consumer groups read at their own pace. That gives decoupling because the producer does not know its consumers, buffering under load, replay because the log retains history, very high throughput, and resilience because a down consumer never fails the producer. The costs are eventual consistency, no synchronous reply, and at-least-once delivery that forces me to make consumers idempotent.

The way I tie it together in my banking work at National Bank of India is that these are complementary, not competing. A single transfer enters over REST because the mobile app needs a universal protocol, debits over gRPC because that internal hop happens millions of times a day and must be fast and typed, and then publishes a payment-completed event over Kafka so notification, audit, and fraud services react asynchronously and new consumers can be added later. So I never standardize on one technology; I choose per interaction, using REST for reach, gRPC for speed, and Kafka for decoupled, replayable fan-out.
